title: Maharashtra's Varkari
hook: a woman at a grinding stone before dawn, singing, and a story that says God sat down and turned the stone with her

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharashtra's Varkari and the palkhi: a saint's sandals carried in a palanquin, so the saint walks with the crowd. Whose way of doing something came along with you? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

It's still dark. A woman sits at a grinding stone, the heavy round kind turned by hand, and the grain goes in a little at a time. It's slow work, and to keep the rhythm she sings. That's Janabai, remembered as a servant in Namdev's household. And the story Varkaris tell about her is that one morning, when the work was too much, Vitthal himself sat down beside her and took the handle, and the two of them turned the stone together, while she sang. Today, the songs of the road, and who was allowed to sing them.
screen: `A GRINDING STONE BEFORE DAWN.` → `JANABAI, SINGING.` → `GOD TAKES THE HANDLE.`

segments.voice: The songs the Varkaris sing on the road are called abhangs: short verses in Marathi, made to be sung with cymbals and a drum, in call and answer. One voice leads, the dindi answers, and the line goes round and round until the whole group is carrying it. Here's what stands out about who made them. Jnaneshwar was born to a family the village had cast out. Namdev was from a family of tailors. Tukaram kept a grocery. And Janabai, by tradition, ground grain and carried water in someone else's house. Her songs speak to Vitthal with startling closeness; some tell him he's late, some call him mother, and the grinding-stone story says he answered by working beside her. Then there's Chokhamela. Tradition remembers him as a Mahar, from a community kept outside the temple, so he sang to Vitthal from beyond its walls. Some of his songs ask, plainly, why the body others call impure should be shut out, when it holds the same God. His abhangs are still sung on the road. So the songs that carry the Varkari walk were made, in good part, by people who could not have stood in front of a priest and been heard. On the road, their voices lead the singing. And now, as this week closes, look back over it. The week opened in Bengal, with Ramakrishna's cat and the Bauls' bird in the cage, where the Mother and Krishna are sung side by side. Then we went west, to Maharashtra: the walk to Pandharpur, Pundalik's brick, the tender word mauli, the saints' sandals in the palkhi, and now the songs themselves, sung by grocers, tailors and servants.
screen: `ABHANGS: SONGS FOR WALKING` · `JANABAI AT THE GRINDSTONE` · `CHOKHAMELA OUTSIDE THE WALLS` · `A WEEK ON THE ROAD`

segments.voice: Sit, and rest your hands on your knees. Bring to mind one plain, repeated job you do: washing dishes, folding laundry, typing, driving. Feel its rhythm in your body. Now breathe in that rhythm, slowly, as if the job were a song. If a line of a song you love comes to you, let it hum quietly inside. If you pray, you can imagine, as Janabai's story does, that you aren't doing that job alone. The bell holds the time.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The tradition whose road songs were made by a servant at a grindstone, a tailor, a grocer, and a man kept outside the temple. Today's word.
